title: Jahanshah Qaraqoyunlu Manuscript Witness Census

creators.name: Kazemipourleilabadi, Negar
creators.affiliation: Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Department of Art History

description:
This dataset records manuscript witnesses for the dispersed Dīvān tradition of Jahanshah Qaraqoyunlu (d. 872 AH / 1467 CE; pen name Ḥaqīqī / Hakîkî). It also documents an LLM-assisted search workflow for building a census across inconsistent multilingual catalogues, printed references, private and community archives, blocked or non-searchable portals, and lost or unlocated reports.

The census records 7 verified and 2 caveated Jahanshah witnesses: 5 on the TEIS Yesevi roster, 1 institutional fragment, and 3 Alevi shrine witnesses in the Ocak tradition: 1 Anatolian (Diyarbakır Ulutürk) and 2 Iranian Azerbaijani (Ilkhchi Kırklar Ocağı). It also records 1 attribution-disputed candidate and 1 lost-attested entry (Diyarbakır YE per Cunbur 1999). Routine search false positives are kept in the per-session search JSONs under data/searches/, outside the witness table. It includes a 257-string search-key matrix: 99 base author/title/context/scribe/Nesimi strings, 106 additional script-family variants, 12 South Asian homonym-disambiguation queries, and 40 Alevi-community route/contact terms. The matrix covers 14 language/script or orthographic traditions: modern Latin, Turkish/Ottoman Turkish, French and German Orientalist forms, Persian/Arabic-script forms, Russian Cyrillic, Azerbaijani Latin/Cyrillic, Georgian, Uzbek Latin/Cyrillic, Tajik Cyrillic, Devanagari, and Urdu nastaliq. The release also includes 5 tezkire or tezkire-adjacent reference extracts and 5 research-log extracts on Hakîkî where available.

The Alevi shrine corpus records eleven published ghazals from Anatolian and Iranian Azerbaijani Ocak traditions that are absent from the institutional editions checked here. It also reports a complete, unphotographed divan codex in the Ilkhchi archive.

The deposit includes 37 indexed search-session and action records, the search-key matrix, search-surface counting rules, false-positive classifications, and a recovery agenda for blocked, private, and on-site manuscript sources. LLM tools assisted search-term expansion, catalogue-variant reconciliation, homonym checking, false-positive logging, and access-gap mapping; witness classifications and attribution decisions remain source-based and human-reviewed. Known failure modes for this use case include over-definitive coverage claims, wrong shelfmarks for real manuscripts, and hallucinated bibliographic entries; human source review and cross-model LLM review were used to mitigate those risks before public claims were retained.
